title: Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Crow
summary: Test data for a differently configured boat and general promotional praise did not establish the specific speed warranty asserted for Crow’s boat.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of Virginia (1999).

The implied-warranty part of the opinion is expressly omitted by the editors at C&M p. 8. The historical references to Article 2 and its enactment belong to this casebook’s account.

257 Va. 121, 509 S.E.2d 499 (1999). The boat reached only 13 mph on delivery (about 17 mph after repairs) against the 30 mph shown in the prop matrixes; the trial court had awarded Crow $135,000 plus prejudgment interest, and the Supreme Court of Virginia reversed on the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness as well as on the express warranty.

sections.Parties: John Crow bought a Bayliner sport-fishing boat through Tidewater Yacht Agency. He sued Tidewater, Bayliner Marine, and the engine manufacturer. The assigned appellate discussion focuses on the judgment against Bayliner.
sections.Material Facts:
Crow briefly piloted a 3486 Trophy Convertible before buying it but could not test its speed. Asked about maximum speed, the dealer’s representative supplied Bayliner’s propeller tables. They listed 30 miles per hour with particular propellers and approximately 600 pounds of passengers and equipment. Crow’s boat had a different propeller. His $120,000 purchase also included approximately 2,000 pounds of extra equipment, including navigation equipment, a generator, and air conditioning. He did not test the completed configuration before delivery.

Crow also saw a brochure stating that the model delivered the performance needed to reach offshore fishing grounds. On delivery, his instruments indicated only 13 miles per hour. Repairs and adjustments followed; the boat generally reached about 17 miles per hour, with a temporary improvement after an engine modification. Speed mattered because the fishing grounds described at trial were roughly 90 miles offshore. Crow said the limited speed defeated his intended use.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the trial court entered judgment against Bayliner for breach of express and implied warranties. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Virginia reviewed the evidence favorably to Crow, the prevailing party below, but reversed and entered final judgment. The casebook omits the opinion’s implied-warranty analysis.
sections.Issue: Did the propeller tables or the brochure create an express warranty that the particular boat sold to Crow would travel at 30 miles per hour?
sections.Holding: No. The tables described a materially different configuration, and the brochure’s general praise did not promise a specific performance characteristic.
sections.Reasoning:
Under UCC § 2-313, an affirmation, promise, or description can create an express warranty when it relates to the goods and becomes part of the basis of the bargain. The court compared the representation to the item actually purchased. Unlike a description identifying the grade of the particular diamonds in another case, the test tables concerned different propellers and substantially lighter equipment. Their qualifications were central to what they represented.

The brochure presented another problem: it expressed general confidence in the boat’s suitability for offshore fishing without specifying a maximum speed. The Code distinguishes such commendation from a factual warranty. Crow’s genuine need for speed and disappointment with the boat did not supply a specific promise absent from these communications. The result illustrates why a buyer’s intended use, a seller’s express representations, and warranties supplied by law must be analyzed separately.

Scope limit: p. 8 states that discussion of the merchantability and particular-purpose warranty claims is omitted. The disposition is reported, but the omitted analysis is not imported from another source.

sections.Parties: Crow bought a Bayliner sport-fishing boat and sued its manufacturer, Bayliner Marine Corporation.
sections.Material Facts: Crow relied on performance materials and statements about the boat’s suitability for offshore fishing. The speed chart concerned a boat with different propellers and a lighter load. Crow’s boat carried substantial additional equipment. Its actual speed disappointed him, and he asserted express and implied warranty theories.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for Crow after a bench trial. The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed and entered final judgment for Bayliner. The casebook expressly omits the appellate discussion of implied warranties, so this brief does not reconstruct that reasoning.
sections.Issue: Did the statements and performance chart amount to affirmations of fact or descriptions, relating to the boat actually bought, that became part of the basis of the bargain?
sections.Holding: The materials did not establish the claimed express warranty. The performance chart described a differently configured boat, and the general statements were opinions or commendations rather than the specific performance assurance alleged.
sections.Reasoning: UCC § 2-313 distinguishes an affirmation of fact or description forming part of the basis of the bargain from the seller’s opinion or commendation. The court analyzes what the representations actually describe, rather than treating every advertised figure as an assurance about every configuration. A chart for different propellers and loading does not by itself warrant Crow’s boat’s speed. The notes contrast an express statement that diamonds are of a stated grade with general praise of a product.

learning.why: Bayliner teaches how to identify the precise undertaking before asking whether performance breached it. The absence of the asserted express warranty does not itself explain every possible implied-warranty claim.

topics.promises: The court identifies the content and limits of a claimed assurance.
topics.warranties: An express warranty must relate to the actual goods and the bargain.
topics.governing-law: The court applies the sales statute rather than relying solely on general common-law promise analysis.
topics.interpretation: Qualifications and product configuration determine what the representation means.
topics.promise-or-prediction: The brochure language was puffery rather than a promise, the distinction this concept addresses.
topics.warranty-overview: The case applies UCC 2-313 express warranty by affirmation of fact and, in the omitted portion, the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness.
